title: Digital Social Work Practice
reference_framework: NASW/ASWB technology standards; IFSW ethical principles

modules.title: Digital inclusion and service design
modules.outcome: Choose an accessible service route with the person, based on their access, preferences, privacy and support needs.

teaching_points.text: A shared phone can create access and privacy barriers even when a person technically owns or borrows a device.
Test a proposed channel with people affected by access barriers before scaling it; a staff-only test misses real usage conditions.
An alternative route should provide a comparable opportunity to use a service, not a punitive or indefinitely delayed option.
Ask about functional access needs instead of inferring digital ability from age, disability or education.
Measure service completion and abandonment by route, using proportionate data and user feedback; logins alone do not demonstrate inclusion.

modules.title: Information governance and secure practice
modules.outcome: Design a proportionate information-handling plan and identify when local governance advice is required.

teaching_points.text: Before collecting information, specify its purpose, who needs it, how it is protected and which locally approved retention rules apply.
Consent discussions should explain the channel's use, foreseeable privacy limitations and available alternatives in understandable language.
An approved channel must still be used appropriately: check the intended recipient and share only necessary information.
A suspected information incident needs prompt action through the organisation's incident route; preserve relevant facts and follow containment instructions.
Retention periods and exceptions require applicable policy and legal review; neither indefinite retention nor immediate deletion is a universal rule.

modules.title: Telepractice, AI, and professional accountability
modules.outcome: Recognise unsuitable digital practice and maintain accountable human judgement when using AI assistance.

teaching_points.text: Telepractice needs a suitability and privacy check plus an agreed response to connection loss or urgent concerns, adapted to the service and local procedures.
Check AI-generated statements against reliable case information; an AI draft is not a verified record or an accountable decision-maker.
Do not enter identifiable case material into an unapproved AI service; use authorised tools and information-governance procedures.
Review differential effects and error patterns before relying on an automated recommendation; average performance can hide exclusion.
A professional should be able to explain and document the reasons for a decision, including how an AI suggestion was checked and when advice was sought.

questions.question: A referral service assumes everyone with a phone can attend a private video appointment. A person shares one phone with several relatives. What should the worker establish first?

options.text: Whether relatives can attend every appointment
Whether a private, affordable and accessible channel is available to that person
Whether the phone is the newest model
Whether video appointments are faster for staff

questions.rationale: Phone access alone does not establish privacy or usability. Device age, staff convenience and family attendance do not resolve the person's access needs.

questions.question: An online intake form works well on staff laptops but residents report difficulty using it. Which pilot would best test inclusion?

options.text: Observe willing users with varied access needs completing representative tasks
Ask the software supplier to confirm that it is modern
Count how many staff members prefer the new design
Launch it everywhere and review only completed forms

questions.rationale: A representative task-based pilot can expose barriers among people unable to complete the form. Successful submissions alone exclude those who dropped out.

questions.question: A learner cannot afford mobile data. The service offers an offline appointment only after all online applicants have been seen. What is the main design problem?

options.text: An offline route automatically prevents confidentiality
Digital and offline routes must use identical equipment
The alternative route introduces unequal access through avoidable delay
The learner must acquire a better phone first

questions.rationale: Comparable access concerns the opportunity and timeliness of service, not identical technology. An alternative should not disadvantage users merely for being offline.

questions.question: A worker assumes an older resident cannot use a digital service. What is the best next step?

options.text: Exclude the resident from digital options
Arrange a family proxy without consulting the resident
Ask the resident about preferences and support needs, then offer suitable choices
Require the resident to demonstrate every phone function

questions.rationale: Individual preferences and practical needs are relevant; age-based assumptions and unnecessary tests can remove choice.

questions.question: A digital service reports twice as many logins after redesign. Which additional information would best test whether access improved?

options.text: The total number of emails sent by the supplier
The colour most frequently used in the interface
Completion and drop-off patterns across access routes, alongside user feedback
The number of devices purchased for managers

questions.rationale: Login volume does not show whether people obtained support. Completion, drop-off and feedback help reveal remaining barriers.

questions.question: A new appointment form requests full family histories although it only schedules a call. Which revision best fits its purpose?

options.text: Ask relatives to submit their records as well
Collect the contact and access details necessary to arrange the call
Require extra identity documents for every enquiry
Retain the full history in case a future project needs it

questions.rationale: The task is scheduling. Unrelated histories add exposure without helping that task; additional data requires a justified purpose.

questions.question: A person signs a generic form but says they do not know who can read messages sent through the service. What should happen next?

options.text: Ask the person to find the platform's technical specification
Explain access and relevant risks, check understanding and revisit the communication choice
Continue collecting sensitive details before discussing access
Treat the signature as proof that every risk was understood

questions.rationale: A signature does not resolve an expressed misunderstanding. The worker should support an informed choice before proceeding with the channel.

questions.question: A worker is about to send a sensitive attachment through an approved system. Two contacts have the same surname. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Verify the intended recipient and the necessary contents before sending
Send it to both contacts to avoid delay
Move the attachment to a personal account
Assume the first autocomplete suggestion is correct

questions.rationale: An approved platform does not prevent a wrong-recipient error. Recipient verification and proportionate disclosure address the immediate risk.

questions.question: A worker discovers that a case attachment went to the wrong recipient. What is the best initial response within role?

options.text: Wait until the next annual review to disclose it
Erase the activity record before anyone sees it
Use the incident-reporting route promptly and follow authorised containment steps
Ask colleagues to keep the event informal

questions.rationale: Reporting enables assessment and containment. Concealing the event or destroying its record can obstruct an appropriate response; notification duties need local advice.

questions.question: A team asks how long all client messages must be kept. What is the appropriate basis for deciding?

options.text: The applicable retention schedule and legal requirements, verified with the responsible lead
A universal seven-day deletion rule for every service
The default setting of whichever phone is used
Unlimited retention because storage is cheap

questions.rationale: The draft cannot prescribe a universal duration. The decision depends on the record purpose and applicable requirements.

questions.question: At the start of a remote appointment the worker learns the person cannot speak privately. What is the best response?

options.text: Continue because the appointment has already started
Require the person to disclose the concern in the shared room
Record the whole household to document the barrier
Discuss a safer suitable channel or time and apply the service's risk procedure if needed

questions.rationale: The absence of privacy changes suitability. A safer arrangement should be considered without forcing disclosure or adding intrusive recording.

questions.question: An AI summary adds a referral that is absent from the verified notes. What should the worker do before using it?

options.text: Keep it because a later worker might make that referral
Ask the person to confirm a referral without disclosing the uncertainty
Accept it because the text sounds professionally written
Check the original information and correct or remove the unsupported statement

questions.rationale: Plausible wording is not evidence. The worker remains responsible for the accuracy of any record they use.

questions.question: A free AI tool asks a worker to paste a named case history to improve a draft. The organisation has not approved the tool. What should the worker do?

options.text: Use an approved workflow and seek governance advice before sharing case information
Remove only the first name and assume the rest is anonymous
Share it and ask permission afterwards
Paste it because the account is password-protected

questions.rationale: A password or partial name removal does not establish an authorised, safe disclosure. Approval and data handling must be considered first.

questions.question: A triage tool performs well overall but frequently misroutes requests written in a minority language. What needs review?

options.text: Whether affected users can be removed from the evaluation
Only whether staff like the dashboard
Only the overall accuracy because it is higher than last year
The unequal error pattern and safer routing options for affected users

questions.rationale: The subgroup pattern identifies a specific access risk. An overall average can conceal it, and excluding affected users would hide the problem.

questions.question: A worker rejects an AI recommendation after finding a factual error. Which record best supports accountability?

options.text: A statement that the computer made the decision
The relevant error, verified information, final reasoning and any consultation
No record because AI was not ultimately followed
Only the final AI confidence score

questions.rationale: A concise reasoning record explains the human decision and its basis; the score alone does not.
